client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just... can't seem to enjoy it the way I used to. Her absence feels like this heavy weight in the room that nobody else seems to notice as much as I do, and honestly I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change how I feel.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — grief has a way of making familiar spaces feel completely different, and it makes sense that her absence weighs on you so heavily, especially when it seems like others around you have moved on more quickly. That feeling of carrying something alone in a crowded room can be incredibly isolating. I also hear a little hesitation in wondering whether talking will even help — can you tell me more about what's making you feel uncertain about that?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I appreciate that you get why it feels isolating, because it really does. It's like everyone else grieved and then just... filed it away, and I'm still stuck carrying this weight around like I can't put it down. As for the uncertainty about talking — I guess I just wonder what words are actually going to do, like, my grandmother is still gone at the end of the session, you know?
therapist: You're absolutely right — no conversation will bring her back, and I'd never want to suggest otherwise. What talking *can* do is help you carry that weight differently, maybe understand why it feels so much heavier for you than it seems to for others, and find a way to stay connected to her memory without it only feeling like pain. What do you think it is about your relationship with her that makes her absence hit you so particularly hard?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think part of it is that she was the one person who never made me feel like a burden. Everyone else in my life, I always have this sense that I'm too much, too anxious, too needy, and she just... didn't seem to see me that way. Now that she's gone, I feel like I lost the only safe place I had, and I don't know how to find that anywhere else.
therapist: What you just shared feels really significant — she wasn't just your grandmother, she was your safe harbor, the one relationship where you could simply exist without editing yourself. Losing that kind of unconditional acceptance is its own particular kind of grief, separate from just missing her as a person. I'm curious — when you say you don't know how to find that safety anywhere else, do you think that feeling of being "too much" is something others have actually told you, or is it more a story you've come to believe about yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think it's both, honestly. There have been moments where people have said things, maybe not directly, but little comments here and there about how I'm "a lot" or how I need to "calm down," and those things stick with you. But you're right that I've probably built a whole story around those moments, like I've taken a few bricks and constructed an entire wall out of them.
therapist: That "bricks into a wall" image is really insightful — you can already see how a handful of painful moments got woven into a much bigger belief about who you are. What's worth noticing is that those comments came from people who may have had their own limitations in understanding you, and your grandmother's experience of you — as someone worth being fully present with — was just as real and valid as theirs. I wonder, if she were here right now, what do you think she would say about this wall you've built?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think she would probably say something like "You don't need to hide yourself, you're enough just as you are." But even imagining her saying that makes my chest tight, because she's gone and I can't actually hear her voice anymore. It's like the one person who really saw me isn't here to remind me, and everyone else just confirms the wall is necessary.
therapist: The way you just spoke her words — "you're enough just as you are" — I can hear how much tenderness and grief are wrapped up together in that. It's a beautiful and painful thing, that the voice you most need to hear is the one you're missing, and yet those words she gave you are still *yours* to keep. I wonder if part of our work together could be about helping you become someone who can remind yourself of what she already knew to be true about you — so that truth doesn't disappear just because she's no longer here to say it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me really wants to believe that's possible. But honestly, when I try to say those words to myself, it just feels hollow — like I'm pretending, or like I'm trying to imitate her and failing. It doesn't feel the same coming from inside my own head as it did coming from her.
therapist: That hollowness makes complete sense — self-compassion that's been modeled by someone else doesn't automatically feel natural when we try to turn it inward, especially when that person is so deeply missed. It's not pretending, though; it's actually a skill that takes time to grow, and right now it probably feels foreign because you've spent so long believing the wall was true. I'm curious — when she said those things to you, did you believe her in the moment, or did part of you resist it even then?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, in the moment I think I half-believed her, like there was this small part of me that wanted so badly for it to be true. But then almost immediately I'd find some reason to dismiss it, like "she only says that because she loves me" or "she doesn't know the real me." It's like I couldn't just let it land without immediately building a case against it.
therapist: What you're describing — that reflex to immediately dismantle any warmth that comes toward you — is actually one of the most common and painful patterns I see, and it tells me the wall has been working very hard to protect itself. It's striking that even the safest person in your life couldn't fully get through without your mind finding a way to block it, which suggests this isn't really about whether people mean what they say — it's about whether you feel worthy of receiving it. What do you think that part of you was so afraid would happen if you just... let her words be true?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I sat with that question for a second and honestly it made my chest feel tight, like you'd just pointed a flashlight at something I didn't want to look at. I think... if I let her words be true, then I'd have to actually believe I'm worth caring about, and then what happens when that gets taken away? It feels safer to never fully accept it in the first place than to let it in and then lose it.
therapist: You just uncovered something really profound — the wall isn't about believing you're unworthy, it's actually a way of protecting yourself from the unbearable risk of losing something precious again, and in a way, losing your grandmother has confirmed that fear in the most painful way possible. That kind of preemptive self-protection makes complete sense as a survival strategy, even as it quietly costs you so much. I want to gently ask — do you think this pattern of keeping good things at arm's length showed up before your grandmother's passing too, or does her loss feel like it's made it harder to let anything in?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, honestly... I think it was there before, but I didn't notice it as much because she was always just there, you know? She was like this safe exception to the rule — I let her in completely, and then she was gone, and it's like that proved something to the part of me that was always waiting for things to fall apart. Now it's like that protective wall has just gotten so much thicker, and I'm more aware of it, but being aware of it doesn't make it easier to take down.
therapist: What you just described — that she was the "safe exception" — is such an important insight, because it means you *are* capable of letting someone in fully, even if that part of you has gone quiet since losing her. And I notice as you're talking about this, there's something that sounds almost resigned in how you say it, like you can see the wall clearly but feel powerless in front of it. I want you to hold onto the fact that awareness really is the first step — not because it magically makes the wall come down, but because you can't choose to walk through a door you can't see.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and yeah, resigned is probably the right word for it. It's just... knowing the wall is there doesn't make it feel any less solid, you know? Like I can see the door, but I have no idea how to make myself want to walk through it when every part of me is convinced something's going to go wrong on the other side.
therapist: The resignation in your words is one thing, but there's something in how you're speaking right now that makes me wonder if underneath that heaviness there's also something more urgent — like a part of you that actually *wants* to find a way through, even as another part insists it's hopeless. That tension between wanting and fearing is actually really important, because it means the door isn't just visible — some part of you is already standing close to it. What do you think it would take for that part of you to feel even a little safer about what might be on the other side?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
